plan: Anti-tell checklist applied. Per-capita data claim, two-clue archaeology inference, restrictive title punctuation, who/whom, literary function of a sentence, synthesis needing evidence plus meaning; S010-08 resubmitted with corrected wording.

passages.title: Lost blueprints
passages.text: Because the bridge's original blueprints had been lost decades earlier, engineers could only ______ how its internal supports were arranged, inferring the layout from patterns of cracks visible on the surface.

passages.title: Childhood kitchen
passages.text:
The following text is from a novel. Teodor is visiting the house where he grew up.
The kitchen was smaller than he remembered. In his mind the table had stood like an island in a wide room, with space enough for his brothers to chase one another around it. Now he could nearly touch both walls by stretching out his arms, and the table, pushed against the window, could seat only three.

passages.title: Library budget
passages.text:
A council member reviewed a city's library budget.
Year | Library budget | City population
2015 | $2.0 million | 100,000
2023 | $2.4 million | 150,000
The council member claimed that, despite the larger budget, the city was spending less on its library per resident in 2023 than in 2015.

passages.title: Distant stone
passages.text: Archaeologists long assumed that the stone tools found at a hilltop site had been made there. Chemical analysis, however, shows that the stone came from a quarry about 300 kilometers away. Moreover, the site contains almost no waste flakes, the small chips that are produced in large numbers whenever stone tools are shaped. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Reef scientist
passages.text: The marine biologist ______ the grant committee selected to lead the new reef survey has studied coral bleaching in the western Pacific for nearly two decades.

passages.title: Carson book
passages.text: Rachel Carson wrote several books about the natural world. Her ______ published in 1962, drew public attention to the dangers of pesticides and helped launch the modern environmental movement.

passages.title: Nurse sharks
passages.text: Many species of shark must keep swimming to push water over their gills and take in oxygen. ______ nurse sharks can rest motionless on the seafloor for long periods, using muscles in their mouths to pump water over their gills.

passages.title: Crow study notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Researchers wore a distinctive mask while trapping and banding several wild crows.
• The crows were then released unharmed.
• In later years, crows on the campus scolded and dived at people wearing that mask.
• The crows largely ignored people wearing a different mask.
• Researchers concluded that crows can recognize and remember individual human faces.

passages.title: Printing press
passages.text: Many histories describe the printing press as a sudden break with the past. Historian Ada Lindqvist disagrees. She points out that for decades before the press, workshops had been producing books by printing from carved wooden blocks, and that early printers deliberately designed their pages to resemble handwritten manuscripts. The press, in her account, sped up changes that were already under way rather than starting them.

passages.title: Glacier notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glaciers in the Arven Range have lost about 40% of their area since 1950.
• Average summer temperatures there have risen by 1.5°C over the same period.
• Researchers attribute most of the glacier loss to longer melt seasons.
• Melt seasons in the range now begin about three weeks earlier than in 1950.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: inferring the layout from patterns of cracks visible on the surface
candidates.explanation: Lacking blueprints, the engineers inferred the layout from indirect clues: they could only "conjecture," or make an educated guess.

A.rationale: Without blueprints they could not confirm the layout; "inferring" signals a guess.

C.rationale: Engineers could not command how the supports were arranged.

D.rationale: The engineers never knew the layout, so they could not remember it.

hints: What does "inferring" suggest about how certain the engineers could be?

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text?

choices.A: It presents Teodor's remembered image, which the third sentence then undercuts.
choices.B: It explains why Teodor's family eventually decided to move out of the house.
choices.C: It describes how the kitchen actually looks to Teodor during his visit.
choices.D: It suggests that Teodor's brothers were often careless and noisy as children.

candidates.evidence: In his mind the table had stood like an island in a wide room
candidates.explanation: "In his mind" marks the second sentence as memory; the third sentence ("Now ...") shows the small reality, undercutting it.

B.rationale: No reason for moving is given.

C.rationale: The second sentence describes the kitchen "in his mind," not as it looks now.

D.rationale: Chasing is a detail of the memory, not a judgment of the brothers.

strategy.explanation: Use the time markers to separate memory from present.

candidates.remember: Literary contrasts often hinge on time markers.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the council member's claim?

choices.A: The library budget rose by $0.4 million, or 20 percent, from 2015 to 2023.
choices.B: The city's population grew by 50 percent from 2015 to 2023.
choices.C: Spending per resident fell from $20 in 2015 to $16 in 2023.
choices.D: Spending per resident rose from $16 in 2015 to $20 in 2023.

candidates.evidence: spending less on its library per resident in 2023 than in 2015
candidates.explanation: Per resident: $2,000,000/100,000 = $20 in 2015 and $2,400,000/150,000 = $16 in 2023, a decrease even though the total budget rose.

A.rationale: This shows the budget grew, which is not the per-resident claim.

B.rationale: Population growth alone does not show spending per resident fell.

D.rationale: This reverses the figures and contradicts the claim.

hints: Divide each year's budget by its population.

strategy.explanation: The claim is about a ratio, so compute the ratio.

candidates.remember: A total can rise while a per-person amount falls.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the tools were shaped somewhere else and reached the site already finished.
choices.B: the residents carried raw stone from the quarry and shaped their tools at the site.
choices.C: the residents of the site did not actually use stone tools in their daily lives.
choices.D: the distant quarry had been abandoned before the hilltop site was occupied.

candidates.evidence: the site contains almost no waste flakes
candidates.explanation: Distant stone shows the material came from far away; the absence of flakes shows the shaping did not happen at the site. Together: finished tools were brought in.

B.rationale: Shaping at the site would have left many waste flakes, which are almost absent.

C.rationale: Tools were found there; the question is where they were made.

D.rationale: Nothing about the quarry's dates is given.

hints: What would be left behind if tools were shaped at the site?

strategy.explanation: Use both clues; eliminate choices that fit only one.

candidates.remember: Combine all the clues before choosing.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the grant committee selected to lead the new reef survey
candidates.explanation: Inside the clause, "the grant committee selected ___": the committee is the subject and the pronoun is the object, so "whom."

A.rationale: The pronoun is the object of "selected" (the committee selected her), so the object form is needed.

B.rationale: "Which" is not used for people in this construction.

D.rationale: "Whose" shows possession, which does not fit.

hints: Rearrange: the committee selected him or he?

strategy.explanation: Use the he/him test inside the clause.

candidates.remember: Whom where him fits; who where he fits.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Rachel Carson wrote several books about the natural world.
candidates.explanation: Because Carson wrote several books, "Silent Spring" is essential and takes no commas; "published in 1962" is extra information set off by a pair of commas.

B.rationale: Because Carson wrote several books, the title is essential to identify which one, so no commas should set it off.

C.rationale: A comma separates the noun from the essential title, and the comma before "published" is missing.

D.rationale: A comma is needed before the descriptive phrase "published in 1962," which closes with a comma.

hints: Did Carson write only one book?

strategy.explanation: The first sentence tells you whether the title is essential.

candidates.remember: Essential titles take no commas; extra details take a pair.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Many species of shark must keep swimming
candidates.explanation: Other sharks must swim to breathe; nurse sharks can rest. The sentences contrast.

A.rationale: Resting motionless is the opposite of having to keep swimming.

B.rationale: The nurse shark's ability is not caused by other sharks' need to swim.

C.rationale: The second sentence describes a different shark, not a restatement.

hints: Is the nurse shark like or unlike the other sharks?

candidates.stem: The student wants to present the study's key finding to an audience unfamiliar with the study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Crows scolded people wearing the mask worn by those who trapped them, suggesting they remember human faces.
choices.B: Researchers wearing a distinctive mask trapped several wild crows, banded them, and released them unharmed.
choices.C: In later years, crows on the campus scolded and dived at some people but largely ignored others.
choices.D: Crows can recognize and remember individual human faces, according to the researchers in the study.

candidates.evidence: Researchers concluded that crows can recognize and remember individual human faces.
candidates.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs both what happened (crows scolded wearers of the trappers' mask) and what it means (they remember faces). Only A gives both.

B.rationale: This describes the method, not the finding.

C.rationale: Without the masks, this does not explain what the crows recognized.

D.rationale: This states the conclusion without the evidence an unfamiliar audience needs.

hints: What does an unfamiliar audience need to understand the finding?

strategy.explanation: Check for both the observation and the conclusion.

candidates.remember: A finding for a new audience needs evidence and meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes an invention, explains how it worked, and lists the earliest books it produced.
choices.B: It compares two historians' accounts and concludes that both of them are partly correct.
choices.C: It gives a common view, introduces a historian who disputes it, and summarizes her evidence and account.
choices.D: It presents a historian's claim and then explains why most other historians reject it.

candidates.explanation: Sentence 1: common view; sentence 2: Lindqvist disagrees; sentence 3: her evidence; sentence 4: her alternative account.

A.rationale: No technical explanation or list of books is given.

B.rationale: Only one historian's view is presented against a general view.

D.rationale: The text never says other historians reject Lindqvist's view.

candidates.remember: Structure answers must fit every sentence in order.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why the Arven Range glaciers have shrunk. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: According to researchers, glaciers in the Arven Range have lost about 40% of their area since 1950.
choices.B: Researchers attribute most of the loss to longer melt seasons, which now start three weeks earlier.
choices.C: Average summer temperatures in the Arven Range have risen by 1.5°C since 1950.
choices.D: In the Arven Range, melt seasons now begin about three weeks earlier than they did in 1950.

candidates.evidence: Researchers attribute most of the glacier loss to longer melt seasons.
candidates.explanation: Only B links a cause (longer melt seasons, starting three weeks earlier) to the effect (glacier shrinkage).

A.rationale: This states the effect without giving a cause.

C.rationale: This is related, but it never connects warming to the glaciers.

D.rationale: This gives the change but does not link it to glacier loss.

hints: Which choice connects a cause to the glaciers?

strategy.explanation: An explanation must link cause and effect.

candidates.remember: Explanations connect a cause to its effect explicitly.
candidates.revision_note: S010-08 resubmitted: key reworded to match the notes exactly (longer melt seasons, which now begin about three weeks earlier), as a blind solver suggested.
